title: Acme Robotics - POC capacity & autoscale scoping
next_steps: Jordan to share proposed GPU sizing and cost estimate by 2025-02-24
Priya to draft POC plan with benchmarking matrix and success criteria by 2025-02-25
Maya to provide sample workload traces and peak qps by 2025-02-22
Schedule 1-hr benchmark kickoff with Acme infra team week of 2025-02-26
action_items: Jordan Hayes: send Dedicated vs Hosted cost comparison + reserved capacity proposal (due 2025-02-24)
Priya Nair: create benchmark matrix (latency, throughput, tails, cost) and test scripts (due 2025-02-25)

summary: POC scoping focused on sizing reserved GPUs for a 6-week pilot, autoscaling/burst strategy for traffic spikes, fallback policies to hosted models, and benchmark plan. Action items assigned to both Redwood and Acme for trace handoff and cost estimates.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-02-20 15:00 PST | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Alex Torres (Redwood SE), Sam Ortega (Acme CTO), Maya Patel (ML Eng), Liam Chen (Infra), Rebecca Yu (Product)

[00:00] Jordan Hayes: hey everyone, thanks for carving time. quick intro - Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account; priya and alex will handle the technical deep dive on capacity and autoscaling. how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Sam Ortega: good, thanks. we want to make sure the POC shows predictable latency during our demo window and keeps cost under control.
[00:15] Priya Nair: great, that's exactly what we'll scope today — reserved GPU sizing, burst capacity, autoscale policies, and fallback behavior. quick ask: can you share your expected qps and typical sequence lengths?
[00:28] Maya Patel: sure — baseline is around 120 requests/minute during business hours, peak demo bursts up to 1500 reqs/min for ~10-15 minutes during launches. most requests are short: 80-150 tokens generated, but we have some long-form generation up to 1.2k tokens for reports.
[00:46] Alex Torres: got it, that's helpful. do you shard work across endpoints today or is it a single endpoint?
[00:52] Liam Chen: single endpoint for now; we route model variants in-app but not at the edge. infra wise we can provide VPC peering and we have strict egress policies — keys must live in our KMS.
[01:05] Priya Nair: sounds typical. for a 6-week POC we usually recommend a reserved pool sized for baseline throughput plus headroom — so capacity to handle 1.5x normal qps with autoscale to handle short bursts. but because you have very short, large bursts to 1500 rps, we'll discuss burst policy options: reserved reserved GPUs with burst queue (pre-warmed) or fallback to hosted variants.
[01:28] Maya Patel: what does pre-warmed mean operationally — is it just extra reserved instances sitting idle?
[01:33] Priya Nair: we can pre-warm GPU workers in the Dedicated pool so cold-starts are minimized. that does have cost; we balance that with burst credits and overcommit strategies. Redwood Dedicated supports a small burst buffer that keeps a slice of capacity warm for X minutes. you can configure burst size and max burst duration.
[01:49] Sam Ortega: and if you exhaust burst capacity? we don't want errors during a demo.
[01:54] Jordan Hayes: two fallback patterns: 1) automatic fallback to a compatible hosted model variant with lower resource needs (quantized or smaller model) to preserve availability while degrading fidelity; 2) queueing with graceful backpressure and user-friendly messaging. we can also route high-cost long-form jobs to a separate queue to avoid impacting low-latency requests.
[02:15] Maya Patel: can you guarantee latencies? our success criteria are p95 < 350ms for short prompts and tail p99 under 800ms during normal load.
[02:24] Priya Nair: for short prompts that target is reasonable on a 80–100ms token generation path depending on model. p95 < 350ms is achievable with the right GPU class and batching config. we'll propose both M40-equivalent (example) and A10/A100-class profiles for the POC.
[02:40] Alex Torres: to put numbers to it — if baseline is 120 req/min and peak bursts 1500 req/min for 10 minutes, we recommend reserving capacity to handle 180 req/min sustained (1.5x baseline) and allowing autoscale to add N burst workers to reach the peak. for the POC, we typically size reserved GPUs to handle steady traffic and provision 2–4 burst units depending on model footprints.
[03:02] Liam Chen: what about sequence length differences? long-form 1.2k token requests will chew memory and reduce concurrency.
[03:08] Priya Nair: exactly. we model workload mix: e.g., 90% short (<=150 tokens) and 10% long (>=1k). during benchmarking we run mixed workload scenarios; long requests reduce throughput per GPU by ~4–6x depending on kv-cache and quantization. we'll include quantized model runs in the benchmark matrix to estimate cost/throughput tradeoffs.
[03:28] Sam Ortega: ok, so what's the POC success criteria we should agree on?
[03:32] Priya Nair: propose: 1) functional: model outputs meet your quality bar on 10 golden prompts (we'll co-author), 2) perf: p95 latency < 350ms for short prompts, p50 < 150ms, 3) throughput: handle 1.5k tokens/sec aggregate for 1 hour sustained in the test run, 4) cost: end-to-end inference cost below your threshold — we'll put exact number in the cost estimate. 5) security: VPC peering and KMS integration validated.
[04:03] Maya Patel: that seems reasonable. can we add warm-start time metric? we care about 95th wake-up time after idle.
[04:10] Alex Torres: yes — include cold-start tail under 2s for pre-warmed units, and warm-start under 500ms.
[04:17] Jordan Hayes: timeline: if we get your traces by 2025-02-22, Redwood will spin up a bench environment and run an initial matrix within 3 business days, share results, then iterate. POC target: 6 weeks starting 2025-02-28. does that align?
[04:31] Sam Ortega: aligns with our demo schedule. we need ROI numbers for execs though — can you produce cost per 1M tokens at both hosted and dedicated configs?
[04:39] Jordan Hayes: yes — we'll include Hosted vs Dedicated delta and reserved commit options. we'll show sample unit economics for your workload mix and expected savings with pre-warmed reserved capacity.
[04:48] Maya Patel: about autoscale mechanics — do you scale by worker count or GPU shard? and what's the granularity/latency of scale events?
[04:55] Priya Nair: we scale worker processes behind the runtime and can add GPU workers within ~30–90s depending on model load and pre-warm policy; burst pre-warm shortens that. autoscale policies are metric-driven: request qps, queue length, token/sec. you can also set absolute caps to avoid runaway cost.
[05:12] Liam Chen: can we set policy to prefer local Dedicated capacity, then fallback to Hosted in another region if Dedicated is exhausted? we want data residency maintained.
[05:22] Alex Torres: yes, routing policies support tiered fallbacks: Dedicated -> Dedicated burst pool -> Hosted in same region -> Hosted in other region. we can annotate each fallback for audit logs so you know when requests hit hosted variants.
[05:37] Rebecca Yu: audit logs and SSO are big for us — will the POC include SAML/SSO and RBAC tests?
[05:44] Jordan Hayes: we can validate SSO and RBAC in the Private control plane during the POC; for Hosted API we demonstrate token-level access and log exports. SOC2 artifacts and KMS architecture will be provided.
[05:55] Maya Patel: what models do you recommend? we currently evaluate a 13B optimized model and a 70B variant for long-form.
[06:02] Priya Nair: for latency-first endpoints we recommend quantized 13B on A10-class or similar; for long-form and fidelity, a 70B with KV-cache and chunked generation on A100 or higher. we'll benchmark both and quantify cost.
[06:17] Sam Ortega: and how do you handle multi-tenancy on Dedicated? we need isolation guarantees for our data in the POC.
[06:24] Alex Torres: Dedicated provides isolated GPU pools and VPC peering; data at rest can be kept in your KMS and logs delivered to your S3. we'll document the boundaries in the POC runbook.
[06:36] Jordan Hayes: next, benchmarking plan: we will run three phases — baseline (steady-state at 1.5x baseline), burst (simulate 1500 rpm bursts, 10–15m), and long-form mix (10% long). metrics: p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, cold-start tail, cost per 1M tokens.
[06:56] Maya Patel: what tooling do you use for load synthesis?
[07:00] Priya Nair: we use a combination of Locust-style runners with real traces you provide; we also instrument the runtime so we can correlate request traces to latency buckets in the dashboard.
[07:10] Sam Ortega: any gotchas we should be aware of?
[07:13] Priya Nair: two common ones: 1) long requests reduce concurrency significantly; if you mix big and small without separate queues, tail latency for short prompts suffers. 2) cold-starts matter — pre-warm or use warm pools for low-tolerance apps.
[07:27] Liam Chen: regarding cost caps, can we enforce a hard cap so POC doesn't explode cost during a runaway test?
[07:32] Alex Torres: yes — we can set per-deployment spend caps and soft alerts. we'll also provide a predicted cost envelope before running heavy benchmarks.
[07:41] Jordan Hayes: recap and next steps — Jordan: send Dedicated vs Hosted pricing and reserve proposal by Monday 2025-02-24; Priya: benchmark matrix and scripts by Tuesday 2025-02-25; Maya: traces by 2025-02-22; schedule kickoff bench week of 2025-02-26. we'll aim to start POC 2025-02-28.
[07:59] Sam Ortega: sounds good, thanks. any final Qs?
[08:03] Maya Patel: one small ask: include explicit measurement for failure modes — e.g., when fallback to hosted happens, dump sample outputs to confirm acceptability.
[08:12] Priya Nair: yes we will — benchmark will capture fidelity delta and we can include a short A/B eval set for the fallback path.
[08:20] Jordan Hayes: great. thanks everyone, we'll follow up in the next 48h with the docs.

[End of transcript]
